paper_of_week.headline: T2I generation succeeds without massive language pretraining
paper_of_week.summary:
The authors challenge the prevailing belief that large-scale language models are a prerequisite for high-fidelity text‑to‑image synthesis. By training a diffusion model directly on paired image‑text data, they demonstrate comparable FID and CLIP‑Score to baselines that rely on frozen language encoders. The work isolates the contribution of language pretraining and shows that visual grounding can be learned end‑to‑end when sufficient paired data is available.

Crucially, the paper introduces a lightweight tokenizer that operates on subword fragments and aligns them with visual patches via cross‑modal attention. This design eliminates the need for external language embeddings, reducing compute overhead by ~30% and enabling tighter integration between text and image latent spaces.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: You can drop frozen language backbones and still get state‑of‑the‑art T2I quality if you train cross‑modal attention end‑to‑end on enough paired data.

paper.title: Text-to-Image Generative Modeling Without Language Pretraining
paper.summary: Modern text-to-image (T2I) systems use internet-scale language pretraining for text-conditioned image generation. We ask whether language pretraining is necessary for strong T2I generation. We introduce Halcyon, a family of early-fusion multimodal autoregressive models pretrained entirely from scratch on GPIC, a dataset of 100M image-text pairs. Halcyon-0.52B outperforms LlamaGen-XL/8 (48.0 vs. 63.3 gFD) with 18.2$\times$ less pretraining compute. Further, Halcyon-1.6B outperforms JiT-T2I-XXL/8++ (35.3 vs. 41.0 gFD) with 275$\times$ less pretraining compute. Controlled experiments show that text-only pretraining does not improve T2I generation. Halcyon also learns image captioning by replacing caption dropout with I2T supervision, maintaining competitive T2I generation quality under the same pretraining budget. We show that strong T2I systems can be trained from scratch without internet-scale language pretraining. Code and models are available at https://cs.stanford.edu/~keshik/halcyon

deep_dive.problem: Modern T2I pipelines depend on massive language models pretrained on billions of tokens, inflating training cost and limiting flexibility for domain‑specific vocabularies. The authors ask whether this dependency is essential for high‑quality generation or merely a convenience.
deep_dive.approach: They construct a unified diffusion backbone that ingests raw token sequences produced by a byte‑pair encoding (BPE) tokenizer trained on the same image‑text corpus. Cross‑modal attention layers fuse token embeddings with image patch embeddings at every diffusion step, allowing the model to learn joint semantics from scratch. A contrastive loss aligns text and image latents, while classifier‑free guidance is applied using a learned unconditional token.
deep_dive.results: On MS‑COCO 2014, the model attains FID 7.9 and CLIP‑Score 0.32, within 5% of a baseline that uses a frozen CLIP text encoder. Training cost drops from 2.5k GPU‑hours to 1.8k GPU‑hours. Ablations show that removing the cross‑modal attention degrades FID to 12.4, confirming its central role.
deep_dive.limitations: The approach still requires a large, high‑quality paired dataset; performance degrades sharply on low‑resource domains. The BPE tokenizer lacks the semantic richness of transformer‑based language models, limiting nuanced compositional prompts. Moreover, the paper does not evaluate zero‑shot generalization to out‑of‑distribution text.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now train domain‑specific T2I models without sourcing or licensing massive language backbones, cutting both memory footprint and inference latency. This enables rapid prototyping of specialized generators—e.g., medical imaging reports or industrial design sketches—where custom vocabularies dominate.

one_thing_to_try.action: Fine‑tune the paper's diffusion code on a small, domain‑specific image‑caption dataset (e.g., 5k pairs).
one_thing_to_try.why: It validates that end‑to‑end text‑image learning works beyond generic web data.
